item.title: Loose coupling between Ca2+ channels and release sensors as a synaptic correlate of higher-order brain function.
item.description:
eLife
In the mature neocortex, functionally distinct areas are built by the same archetypes of neurons, but depending on the area, these neurons and their synapses are engaged in very different functions, ranging from lower-order processing of sensory information to higher-order associations and cognitive functions. We found significant differences in the functional presynaptic nanoarchitectures of the same types of pyramidal neuron synapses, depending on whether they are located in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) or in the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) of mice. Mature synapses in PFC operated with loose microdomain coupling, as opposed to tight nanodomain coupling in S1. These differences were associated with significant differences in synaptic timing, efficacy, and plasticity between areas. Our data suggest that the mature neocortex uses tuning of synaptic topographies to specialize seemingly identical types of neurons for their required function. They suggest that microdomain coupling in pyramidal neuron synapses could be a presynaptic structure-function correlate of higher-order neocortical functions.

item.title: Ultrasound neuromodulation hypotheses on the directionality of effects and community resource.
item.description:
eLife
Low-intensity transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) is a promising non-invasive technique for brain stimulation and focal neuromodulation. Research with humans and animal models has raised the possibility that TUS can be biased towards enhancing or suppressing neural function. Here, we first collate a set of hypotheses on the directionality of TUS effects and conduct an initial meta-analysis on available healthy human participant TUS studies reporting stimulation parameters and outcomes (n=47 studies, 52 experiments). In initial exploratory analyses with univariate tests, we find that parameters, such as the intensity and continuity of stimulation (duty cycle, DC) show statistical trends towards likely TUS neural enhancement or suppression of function. Machine-learning analyses were limited by the currently small sample size. Given that human TUS sample sizes are expected to increase, predictability on the directionality of TUS effects could improve if a database is available. Therefore, we establish an inTUS database and resource for the systematic reporting of TUS parameters and outcomes to assist in greater precision in TUS use for brain stimulation and neuromodulation. The paper concludes with a selective review of human clinical TUS studies illustrating how hypotheses on the directionality of TUS effects could be developed for empirical testing in the intended clinical application, not limited to the examples provided.

item.title: The interplay between cortical tracking and functional connectivity in musicians and non-musicians listening to speech and music
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Musical expertise is associated with auditory processing advantages which can extend to the speech domain. However, the origins of such domain-general benefits remain unclear. Recent frameworks propose that better rhythm processing in musicians might be at the basis of the observed advantages in processing music and speech. Auditory cortical tracking and inter-regional interactions between auditory and motor areas have been proposed as key neural mechanisms. In this study, we asked whether expertise-related increase in cortical tracking would be elicited by naturalistic stimuli in clear listening conditions, and whether such effects would be related to audiomotor functional connectivity and individual rhythmic abilities. We compared MEG data from expert musicians and controls with no musical playing experience while they listened to two-minutes long stories and excerpts of piano music. We also collected behavioral data in a rhythmic task testing speech (syllable) production. We found that musicians showed enhanced tracking and enhanced functional connectivity in both speech and music conditions, as well as better rhythmic abilities relative to non-musicians. Alpha connectivity between the right auditory cortex and inferior frontal gyrus negatively predicted cortical tracking across all participants in the speech condition, while no relation was observed for music. We suggest that stronger cortical tracking in musicians is due to domain-general differences in auditory sensory processes and is not driven by motor influences in our experiment. Moreover, a trade-off between cortical tracking and inter-regional communication might be at the basis of optimal perception of speech in both musicians and non-musicians in clear listening conditions.

item.title: Claustrum Morphometry Reveals Spatially Heterogeneous Alterations in 22q11DS
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The human claustrum is a small, irregular, and complexly positioned structure, yet it carries long range projections to most cortical regions responsible for executive functioning. Prior structural MRI research has largely relied on global volume as the metric of its morphology. Such measures may obscure regionally specific morphological changes relevant to developmental and pathological variation. We therefore addressed this limitation by applying longitudinal surface-based morphometry to 874 scans from 440 individuals aged 5-35 years, comparing typical development with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22q11DS), a genetic condition characterized by brain dysmaturation, and assessing associations with working memory performance. Our data show a significant age-related volumetric decline that is reduced in 22q11DS left claustra, while surface deformation and thickness analyses revealed spatial patterns unique to hemisphere, group, and developmental age. In controls, the claustrum surface deformed with age in clustered zones along a dorsoventral gradient, and the dorsal-anterior zone thinned across development while the ventral zone thickened. 22q11DS claustra showed less age-related deformation than controls, whose claustrum surface changes associated with verbal working memory. This structural correlate was statistically equivalent to zero in carriers, consistent with a disrupted claustral development to the working memory vulnerability of the syndrome. These findings show the value of surface‑based morphometry over volume alone, highlight dysmaturation and regionally organized claustrum shape variation, and suggest that disrupted structural organization is accompanied by a weaker claustrum-working memory association.

item.title: Naturalistic Movie Viewing Reveals a Distributed Network Supporting Audiovisual Speech Processing
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Traditional paradigms in cognitive neuroscience often fail to capture the richness of real-world experiences. To bridge this gap, researchers increasingly use naturalistic stimuli such as movies, which provide complex, multisensory input. Speech perception is a prime example of such complexity: it is inherently multisensory, involving the integration of auditory cues, lip movements, and facial expressions. Prior studies suggest that the left posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) and superior temporal gyrus (STG) play a critical role in this integration. However, most studies of audiovisual speech have relied on simplified or artificial stimuli, limiting ecological validity. To address these gaps, we analyzed fMRI data from human participants watching two full-length films (500 Days of Summer, Citizenfour) to assess the consistency of multisensory speech processes across distinct genres and narratives. We manually annotated word onset times and modality (audiovisual vs. auditory-only). Across two movies and 38 participants we observed consistent speech-related activation in the pSTS and STG across speech types. Compared to auditory-only speech, audiovisual speech recruited a broad left-lateralized network including the angular gyrus, posterior temporal cortex, temporal pole, and inferior frontal gyrus, along with the right cerebellum. These findings were also consistently present in single-subject data. Importantly, most of the regions observed in our analyses have been implicated in multisensory function in the nonhuman primate literature despite receiving relatively little focus in human neuroimaging. Together our results demonstrate that speech processing during naturalistic viewing recruits a distributed network extending substantially beyond regions traditionally emphasized in audiovisual speech research.

item.title: Brain Dynamics of Persistent Postural-Perceptual Dizziness at Rest Reveal Alterations in Multisensory and Motor Areas
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background: Persistent Postural-Perceptual Dizziness (PPPD) is a chronic functional disorder with unsteadiness and postural instability, attributed to altered multisensory integration and visual dependence. fMRI studies report altered connectivity in several regions, however, dynamic connectivity remains unexplored. Objectives We characterized resting-state brain dynamics in 17 patients with PPPD and 20 matched healthy controls (HC), and their relationship to clinical and postural measures. Methods Co-Activation Patterns (CAPs) were derived from resting-state fMRI scans for four seeds relevant to multisensory integration, motor output and vestibular processing - right temporo-parietal junction (rTPJ), caudate nucleus, hippocampus and operculo-parietal area 2 (OP2) - and their temporal metrics compared between groups. Partial Least Squares Correlation (PLSC) related CAPs to mood, vertigo, stress, and visual dependence for gait and postural control. Results Patients with PPPD showed altered dynamics seeded from rTPJ (decrease of a salience-coupled CAP, increased entries into a visual/dorsal-attention-coupled CAP), caudate nucleus (increased time in a default mode-coupled CAP, decrease of a salience/visual-coupled CAP) and hippocampus (increase of a default-mode-coupled CAP), but not OP2. PLSC yielded two significant latent components: the first linked rTPJ, OP2 and hippocampal CAPs sharing visual network co-deactivation to stress, mood, vertigo and visual dependence for gait; the second linked all caudate and two rTPJ CAPs to postural sway with eyes closed (visual dependence). Individual brain-behavior scores correlated in both groups. Conclusion Resting-state dynamics are altered in multisensory and motor regions in PPPD, but preserved in OP2, the core vestibular cortex. Brain-behavior organization appears shared across groups, with shifted dynamics in patients.

item.title: Divergence from Diffusion Tensor: a discriminant diffusion marker from single shell MRI
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Purpose: The Divergence from the Diffusion Tensor (DDT) is a new diffusion MRI metric that quantifies how the measured diffusion signal separates from the tensor assumption. It is marker for tissue heterogeneity that is estimated from single-shell data and can be used in brain studies. Methods: There exist other techniques that allow the calculation of how the measured diffusion diverges from the Gaussian and tensor assumptions. However, the calculation requires large data-sets with different b-values, which makes them incompatible which standard diffusion tensor acquisitions. By imposing an initial assumption, an alternative formulation based on one single shell (ie, single b-value) is reported. Results: Publicly available databases are used to test the behavior of DDT against other anisotropy measures. It shows the ability to discriminate different non-Gaussian diffusion scenarios with very low intra-subject variabilities. Conclusions: DDT can extract relevant information from the white matter, without any additional demands on data acquisition and totally compatible with standard diffusion MRI analysis pipelines. This makes DDT a good candidate to be used as an imaging marker for brain studies.

item.title: Impact of Chatbot-Based Cognitive Training on Cognitive Function and White Matter Integrity in Cognitively Unimpaired Older Adults: Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description:
JMIR aging
Cognitive training may enhance cognition and support brain health during aging, but few trials have evaluated readily accessible chatbot-based programs with neuroimaging outcomes. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of a chatbot-based cognitive training program on white matter microstructural organization and cognition in cognitively unimpaired older adults. In a single-blind randomized controlled trial, 72 cognitively unimpaired older adults were assigned to chatbot-based cognitive training (30 min/day, 5 days/week for 12 weeks; n=37) or a no-intervention control (n=35). Diffusion tensor imaging at baseline and 12 weeks quantified fractional anisotropy (FA) in predefined white matter tracts, and cognition was assessed with the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery. Groups were comparable at baseline. After 12 weeks, the training group showed significantly less FA reduction than controls in the bilateral tapetum and right posterior thalamic radiation, surviving false discovery rate control (P<.05). The training group also improved on Paired Associates Learning (PAL), an episodic memory measure (P=.04). PAL improvement was positively associated with FA change in the right posterior thalamic radiation and right sagittal stratum (false discovery rate-adjusted P=.04 for each). These findings suggest that a 12-week chatbot-based cognitive training program may support episodic memory and the relative maintenance of white matter microstructural organization in selected pathways in cognitively unimpaired older adults, consistent with a brain-maintenance framework. CRIS KCT0004630; https://tinyurl.com/4xfesb68.

item.title: Learning from Error Predictions Rather Than Prediction Errors: A Perspective on Self-Supervised Learning in the Brain.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Humans learn by doing and observing but also by imagining the result of simulated actions in their mind. When learning from executed or observed actions, traditional theories posit that behavior improves by minimizing the difference between (1) the perceived outcome derived from sensory feedback and (2) the desired outcome (performance error) or the outcome predicted by an internal model (prediction error, PE). Supporting these theories, decades of electrophysiological studies have documented the role of the dopaminergic system and cerebellum in generating activity patterns compatible with the hypothesized error signals. In comparison, our understanding of the neural basis underlying the ability to learn from simulated actions is far more limited. Here, I argue that this form of self-supervised learning is best described in terms of a quantity known as the predicted performance error (PPE), theorized more than 30 years ago and yet largely overlooked ever since. Complementary to PEs, PPEs reflect "error predictions" between predicted and desired outcomes. Unlike PEs, however, PPEs exist even in the absence of sensory feedback and can in principle serve to evaluate actions without executing them, based on an efference copy of the underlying motor plan. I review evidence supporting the computation of PPEs in the brain and propose a network implementation based on a cortico-basal ganglia loop interacting at multiple timescales with prefrontal, parietal, and hippocampal areas. I then connect PPEs to recent discoveries on motor planning and formulate novel predictions linking PPEs to various high-level brain functions such as metacognition, problem-solving, and deception.

item.title: Individualised electrophysiological neural field models for the assessment of thalamocortical function in disorders of consciousness: A multicentre study.
item.description:
PLoS computational biology
Understanding the neural mechanisms underlying disorders of consciousness (DoC) remains a major challenge, particularly in distinguishing limited awareness in minimally conscious state (MCS) and complete unawareness in unresponsive wakefulness syndrome, also coined vegetative state (UWS/VS). In this multicentre study, we fitted a biophysically informed corticothalamic neural field model to high-density EEG data from two large independent datasets, comprising 203 UWS patients, 270 MCS patients and 74 healthy controls. We then used the fitted parameters to simulate EEG time series on a per-subject basis and compared empirical and simulated complexity metrics. The model reliably captured the spectral features across different states of consciousness and revealed reduced corticothalamic integrity in DoC patients that was more pronounced in UWS than in MCS, supporting the mesocircuit hypothesis. Furthermore, the simulated EEG reproduced the complexity patterns of the empirical recordings, with permutation entropy emerging as a sensitive marker capable of distinguishing between MCS and UWS for both real and simulated time series.

item.title: Emotion regulation capacity lacks a shared neural signature.
item.description:
Nature
Cognitive reappraisal refers to changing how one thinks about a situation to alter its emotional impact. It is central to well-being1 and engages prefrontal regulatory circuits2, prompting the assumption that their activity reflects a person's capacity to regulate emotions3-5. Yet evidence for this assumption remains inconclusive and has not been established at scale. Here we analysed 40 task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) datasets in a preregistered consortium with 2,175 participants and show that three widely used indicators of reappraisal capacity-trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings and amygdala down-regulation-do not converge on a common core. Moreover, none of the three indicators showed the expected association with canonical prefrontal regulatory circuits. Trait questionnaires showed no detectable neural associations across the brain and task-based affective ratings were instead associated with responses in the amygdala and sensorimotor cortices. At the process level, canonical control circuits were engaged during both emotion generation and reappraisal, challenging their presumed specificity for emotion regulation. These findings caution against using activation in putatively regulatory brain regions to infer how well a person regulates emotions, with implications for neural biomarkers, interventions and psychoeducation that link emotion regulation difficulties to specific regional brain deficits.

item.title: Individualized structural brain network and transcriptomic characterization of heterogeneity in type 2 diabetes mellitus.
item.description:
Neuroscience
Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a heterogeneous metabolic disorder that also affects the brain, yet prior neuroimaging studies have predominantly focused on group-level comparisons, obscuring interindividual variability in brain structural organization. To capture this heterogeneity, we constructed individualized differential structural covariance networks for 156 individuals with T2DM using 148 healthy controls as a normative reference. Unsupervised clustering based on these individualized networks revealed two neuroanatomical subtypes with distinct network configurations. Most subtype-differentiating edges showed higher values in one subtype, whereas a smaller set of edges, primarily involving the basal ganglia and cerebellum, showed higher values in the other. Integration with transcriptomic data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas identified genes spatially associated with subtype-related differences. These genes were enriched in processes including receptor tyrosine kinase signaling and glycerolipid metabolism, with preferential expression in the striatum and cerebellum. Together, these findings characterize interindividual variation in brain structural covariance in T2DM and identify candidate molecular processes associated with the observed subtype differences.

item.title: Impact of hearing loss on visual selective attention: Evidence from N2pc and resting-state networks.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Efficient visual attention is fundamental to environmental adaptation and social interaction. While previous studies have observed alterations in visual processing among deaf individuals, findings remain controversial regarding whether these changes stem from hearing loss (sensory compensation vs. cognitive deficit) or sign language experience. To address this issue, the present study provides task-related and resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) evidence to disentangle the specific drivers of visual selective attention plasticity. A visual search task was used to examine selective attention in 95 participants (34 prelingual deaf, 27 hearing signers, and 34 hearing nonsigners). Compared to both hearing groups, deaf individuals exhibited significantly lower hit rates and diminished N2-posterior contralateral (N2pc) amplitudes. Hearing signers and nonsigners showed comparable behavioral performance, N2pc amplitudes, and resting-state network topology, whereas the deaf group was further characterized by a degraded resting-state alpha network topology, evidenced by reduced clustering coefficients, global efficiency, and weakened frontal-occipital connectivity. N2pc amplitude correlated significantly with resting-state network properties and behavioral accuracy. These results suggest that deaf individuals may suffer from an imbalance in the regulation of visual selective attention, most clearly indexed by the evoked N2pc and by intrinsic alpha-network organization, and likely linked to increased resource competition following the loss of auditory monitoring. Our findings provide neurophysiological evidence that these attentional deficits are associated with hearing loss rather than with sign-language experience, offering a new perspective for understanding the boundaries of cross-modal plasticity in the human brain.

item.title: Disrupted gray matter morphological network topology associated with suicide attempts in adolescents with major depressive disorder and bipolar disorder.
item.description:
Journal of affective disorders
Suicide is a leading cause of death among adolescents with major depressive disorder (MDD) and bipolar disorder (BD), yet the suicide-related structural network alteration patterns remain poorly understood. The study investigates the structural network topological alterations and associations with suicide attempts in unmedicated adolescents with MDD and BD. High-resolution T1-weighted MRI data was acquired from 41 healthy controls (HCs), 34 adolescents with BD, and 48 with MDD. Gray matter morphological similarity networks were constructed through the Jensen-Shannon Similarity Estimation. The global and nodal topology were characterized by graph theory. Additionally, a nested 5-fold cross-validation framework was used to classify suicide attempters (SA) and non-suicide attempters (nSA). Compared with HCs, both MDD and BD exhibited lower normalized characteristic path length (λ), whereas MDD showed higher normalized clustering than BD. In within-diagnosis comparisons, BD-SA showed higher λ than BD-nSA. Alterations in nodal topological properties were observed across multiple brain regions in both the MDD and BD. Additionally, in the SA, higher suicidal tendency-wp scores were associated with higher nodal degree and efficiency in the right middle frontal gyrus (orbital part) (p ≤ 0.001). The five fold-specific optimal models distinguished SA from nSA with 79.85% accuracy (AUROC = 0.801), with features from the right inferior frontal gyrus (orbital part), right supplementary motor area, and left Heschl's gyrus contributing most strongly. Exploratory findings suggest regional morphological similarity network patterns are associated with suicide-attempt history in adolescents with MDD and BD. Moreover, network features showed preliminary value for classifying lifetime attempt history.

item.title: Prefrontal Cortical Changes With Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement in Opioid Use Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
item.description:
JAMA psychiatry
Despite decades of clinical implementation of medications for opioid use disorder (OUD), overdose mortality rates remain high, underscoring a critical need for interventions that target the brain mechanisms underlying addiction. To assess the neural mechanisms of Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement (MORE) and their associations with clinical outcomes, including craving and abstinence duration. This randomized clinical trial was conducted from November 2020 to September 2024 among individuals with OUD recruited from an inpatient rehabilitation facility in New York and randomized to MORE or psychoeducational supportive therapy (PST). Data were analyzed from October 2024 to August 2026. Treatment with MORE (comprising training in mindfulness, drug cue reappraisal, and savoring positive experiences) or PST (active control condition) across 8 weekly 2-hour group sessions. Outcomes included treatment-related changes in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) blood oxygen level-dependent signal (primary), abstinence length (secondary), and cue-induced craving (secondary). Drug cue reactivity task analyses included 59 participants (MORE, n = 24; 5 women [20.8%]; mean [SD] age, 43.6 [11.3] years; PST, n = 35; 8 women [22.9%]; mean [SD] age, 42.8 [10.0] years). Movie-watching and follow-up analyses were conducted in subsets of 37 (MORE, n = 18; PST, n = 19) and 38 participants (MORE, n = 13; PST, n = 25), respectively. Compared with PST, MORE reduced drug-biased activity in the middle frontal gyrus and other brain areas, including the precuneus, during downregulation of responses to drug cues relative to upregulation of responses to natural reward cues (even when controlling for passive cue viewing; z > 3.1; P < .05). The shift from drug to natural reward responses in the lateral and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (PFC) was associated with lower cue-induced craving exclusively in the MORE group (z > 3.1; P < .05). Relative to PST, MORE also reduced medial PFC synchronization to naturalistic drug-related movie scenes (q = 0.019) and significantly extended abstinence duration at follow-up (approximately 4 months posttreatment; χ2 = 6.7; P = .04; Cohen w = 0.19). This neuroimaging randomized clinical trial demonstrates that MORE may restructure function in PFC nodes of the reward, salience, and control networks, positioning it as a biologically grounded adjunct to pharmacotherapy for OUD. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04112186.

item.title: Neurotransmitter receptor architecture links local neurochemistry to semantic memory
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
A fundamental challenge in neuroscience is understanding how the molecular and neurochemical architecture of the human cortex gives rise to sophisticated higher cognitive functions. The anterior temporal lobe (ATL) is a key hub for semantic memory, and its underlying GABAergic and glutamatergic neurochemistry supports semantic memory performance. However, the molecular receptor architecture underlying these neurochemical-cognitive relationships remains unknown. Here, we combined imaging transcriptomics and in vivo magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) to investigate how neurotransmitter receptor organisation relates to local neurochemistry and semantic memory in the human ATL. We found that the ATL exhibited a distinct transcriptomically inferred receptor-subunit profile relative to control cortical regions (occipital cortex and vertex). Individual-specific spatial estimates of receptor-subunit gene expression were systematically associated with local GABA+ and Glx concentrations, revealing preferential coupling between GABAergic receptor genes and GABA+ and between glutamatergic receptor genes and Glx, alongside widespread cross-system associations between GABAergic receptor architecture and Glx. ATL GABA+ and Glx concentrations were positively associated with semantic memory performance, and GABAergic and glutamatergic receptor-subunit expression showed selective relationships with semantic memory accuracy. Crucially, mediation analyses revealed that GABA+ mediated associations between GABAergic receptor architecture and semantic performance, whereas Glx mediated both glutamatergic and widespread GABAergic receptor associations. Together, these findings reveal a coupled molecular-neurochemical architecture of the human ATL, linking neurotransmitter receptor organisation to regional neurochemical state and individual differences in semantic memory. Our findings provide a multiscale account of how cortical molecular organisation is associated with human higher cognitive function.

item.title: Microstructure of white matter association tracts in the temporal lobe predicts the timing of electrophysiological activity and behaviour in picture naming
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
White matter (WM) microstructure has been mainly associated with accuracy of picture naming. However, little is known about how WM properties relate to the timing of picture naming and its underlying electrophysiological activity. Here, we linked diffusion-weighted, electrophysiological, and behavioural data, using time-based measures to conceptually connect WM deterioration to alterations in conduction speed and precision. Our sample included individuals of varying age, with or without stroke. We correlated fractional anisotropy (FA) of bilateral WM tracts traversing the temporal lobe with mean response times (RTs) and response time variability (coefficient of variation, CV) in picture naming, and with the onset latency of neuronal activity, represented by the electrophysiological P2 component time-locked to picture onset. We selected tracts showing associations with P2 latency and naming performance separately, on which we conducted path analyses examining the relationship between structure, neuronal activity and behaviour. Depending on the tract, higher FA was associated with faster and/or more consistent naming, suggesting that ventral tracts differentially contribute to naming speed and consistency. Importantly, path modelling for the right inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF) revealed that FA predicted P2 latency, which in turn predicted RTs, possibly reflecting a structure-activity-behaviour relationship in lexical-semantic processing. P2 source reconstruction demonstrated anatomical proximity to posterior segments of the right IFOF, supporting these findings. Overall, this study provides a proof of concept for modelling structure-activity-behaviour relationships in language research, while highlighting the need for elaboration of such relations at a more mechanistic level.

item.title: Older Adults Show Preserved Neural Signatures of Audiovisual Integration but Altered Links to Speech Comprehension
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Older adults often experience difficulty understanding speech in noisy environments despite relatively preserved hearing. Although visual speech cues can improve speech perception, it remains unclear whether the neural mechanisms supporting audiovisual integration are preserved in healthy ageing. We addressed this question using magnetoencephalography (MEG) combined with Rapid Invisible Frequency Tagging (RIFT) during challenging audiovisual speech task. Forty younger and forty older adults attended to one of two competing speech streams while the speaker's lip movements were frequency tagged, with the visual modulation driven by either the attended or unattended speech envelope. Task-Relevant amplitude modulation of frequency tagging in visual speech improved speech comprehension in younger adults as previously reported for this cohort; this accuracy benefit was absent in older adults. Auditory and visual tagging responses were modulated by task relevance similarly across age groups, indicating largely preserved modality-specific sensory processing in older adults. Intermodulation responses, reflecting nonlinear interactions between auditory and visual speech signals, also remained sensitive to task relevance and did not differ in their condition-dependent modulation between age groups. Greater Task-Relevant versus Task-Irrelevant differences in intermodulation coherence were also associated with greater comprehension benefits in younger adults; no significant association was found in older adults, and this relationship differed significantly between age groups. These findings suggest that the absence of a comprehension benefit in older adults is linked to a change in the relationship between audiovisual intermodulation and behaviour, despite largely preserved task-sensitive brain responses.

item.title: Cerebello-basal ganglia networks and behavior across adulthood and aging
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The cerebellum contributes to aging, cognition, and reward related processing, but has been relatively understudied in these domains. The cerebello-basal ganglia (CB-BG) circuit may be key to better understanding how the brain ages. Prior work has implicated this circuit in aging in a small sample, though it is also of interest in age-related neurodegenerative disease, particularly Parkinson's Disease. Here, we investigated the CB-BG network, which has been implicated in modulation of cognitive, motor, and reward-related functions. In a sample of 138 participants between the ages of 35 and 86 we looked at network connectivity in cognitive and motor sub-circuits. Participants completed motor and cognitive testing batteries followed by 26 minutes of resting state functional connectivity magnetic resonance imaging (fcMRI). This data was analyzed using the CONN toolbox with an ROI-ROI approach targeting the CB-BG circuit. We replicated the previously mapped cognitive subcircuit and motor subcircuits. When examining connectivity by age group (early and late middle age and older adult hood), we found higher functional connectivity in early middle age compared to older adulthood, with no results related to late middle age. Analysis of connectivity as it relates to performance on the Stroop task showed higher connectivity-behavior associations in early middle-aged adults compared to older adults. We also explored sex differences and found higher functional connectivity in females compared to males. Analysis of steroid hormone levels revealed higher connectivity associated with progesterone in females relative to males. Together, we have replicated motor and cognitive CB-BG subcircuits and further demonstrated that this network has altered connectivity associated with age, sex, progesterone, and cognitive performance. This expanded investigation of CB-BG networks represents an essential new step in increasing our knowledge of age-related cognitive and motor declines and may be particularly relevant for consideration in Parkinson's Disease.

item.title: Habitual sleep duration is associated with the cortical organisation of brain network controllability
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Sleep is fundamental to adaptive brain function, yet how habitual sleep relates to the structural network properties that support flexible transitions between brain states remains poorly understood. Combining wrist-accelerometer sleep measures with diffusion MRI connectomes from 15,799 UK Biobank adults, we show that longer workday sleep is associated with higher modal controllability of somatomotor systems and lower controllability of visual cortex. This system-specific signature reproduced in a locked test set (n = 4,740) and was robust across extensive sensitivity analyses. Decomposition showed that it reflects a redistribution of structural connection weight, with greater absolute visual connectivity and a smaller somatomotor share of the whole-brain total. Weekend catch-up sleep showed no comparable association. The signature was distinct from brain-ageing patterns and, across 1,226 phenotypes, related mainly to physical activity and body composition rather than cognition. These findings link everyday sleep habits to the system-specific organisation of brain network controllability.

item.title: Insula functional connectivity development follows a canonical antero-posterior axis of organization
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The insula is a heterogeneous region associated with a range of functional domains including sensory, cognitive, and emotional processing. Cytoarchitectural and functional studies have described an antero-posterior axis of insula organization. However, the insula's functional development remains sparsely described. We delineated the development of insula resting-state functional connectivity across 562 individuals (6-22 years) using generalized additive models and population value decomposition. We show insulo-cortical functional connectivity development differs across the insula: anterior subregions have predominantly decreasing connectivity across the age range examined, whereas posterior subregions have variable connectivity that aligns with the sensorimotor-association axis. Vertex-level analysis revealed that age-related trajectories followed an antero-posterior axis that aligned with estimates of insula microstructure. Our results emphasize that the development of insula connectivity is spatially heterogeneous and aligns with known cytoarchitecture. The normative insula development described here provides a foundation for investigating how emerging psychopathology may be linked to variation in insula development.

item.title: Brain Age Gap Associations with Externalising Behaviours in Youth: A Longitudinal Investigation in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Cohort
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Background: Early adolescence is a period of heightened risk for the emergence of externalising psychopathology, making it an important window for identifying neurodevelopmental risk markers. Differences between predicted brain age and chronological age - termed the brain age gap - reflect variation from age-typical patterns of brain structure. While brain age gap has been closely linked with internalising behaviours in adolescence, less is known about its relationship with externalising symptoms. This study examined whether brain age gap in late childhood/early adolescence (9-11 years) is associated with current externalising symptoms and whether it predicts externalising trajectories over seven-year follow-up. Methods. Participants were 10,516 adolescents (aged 9-11 at baseline; up to 18 years at follow-up) from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study who met inclusion/exclusion criteria. Brain age gap for each participant was derived from an external validated prediction model (Drobinin et al., 2022) applied to baseline measurements of cortical volume, area, and subcortical volume. Linear mixed-effects models were used to test cross-sectional and longitudinal associations between baseline brain age gap and externalising symptoms, as assessed using the Child Behaviour Checklist. Primary models were adjusted for age, sex, pubertal status, and prior to inclusion of sociodemographic covariates (ethnoracial identity and caregiver highest education). Results. A higher/more positive brain age gap was associated with greater externalising symptoms at baseline (B[SE]=0.067[0.033], p=.042), but this association was removed following sociodemographic adjustment (B[SE]=0.056[0.033], p=.088). Longitudinally, a significant brain age gap x age interaction was identified that remained evident after sociodemographic adjustment, with this relationship weakening across adolescence (B[SE]=-0.007[0.003], p=.033). Conclusions. These findings suggest that a more positive brain age gap, indicating more mature-appearing brain structure for age, in late childhood/early adolescence may be associated with externalising psychopathology, but this relationship is likely to be age- and context-dependent rather than a stable marker of persistent behavioural risk.

item.title: Familiarity synchronizes brain rhythms during natural viewing
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Our perception of the world is shaped not only by sensory information, but also by prior experience. However, how familiarity alters the coordination of neural representations across distributed brain networks remains unclear. Rhythmic neural activity provides a potential mechanism for coordinating information across sensory and higher-order brain regions in the light of previous experience. Here, we thus investigated whether familiarity alters the coordination of brain rhythms during naturalistic viewing. Participants who were either familiar or unfamiliar with the television series Game of Thrones viewed clips from the series while EEG or fMRI was recorded. We calculated the intersubject correlations of neural activity across EEG frequency bands and related this rhythmic activity to fMRI BOLD responses. Across participants, all brain rhythms showed reliable intersubject synchrony and related to activity across large-scale brain networks. Familiarity selectively enhanced intersubject synchronisation in beta and gamma rhythms, with these effects reflected in visual and default mode brain regions. Moreover, beta and gamma band activity were modulated by similar aspects of the movie, suggesting coordinated familiarity-related processing. These findings show that familiarity selectively shapes rhythmic neural dynamics across the cortex, providing a mechanism through which prior experience alters the coordination of neural representations during naturalistic perception.

item.title: Evaluating the mobile MUSE EEG headband for studying resting state EEG and event-related potentials
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
We examined whether and how tactile EEG experiments could be done through self-assessments by participants at home or through online experiments with consumer-grade mobile EEG devices. As a first step towards this aim, we performed a Flanker task in an online scenario with a MUSE headband and similarly a conventional lab experiment with a standard EEG device.Five undergraduate students participated in a visual flanker experiment and associated ERP components were recorded with either a standard 32-channel EEG System or a 4-channel MUSE EEG headband. In addition, we performed a 2-minutes resting state recording.Resting state brain oscillations measured with the Muse device revealed a similar pattern as with a standard EEG machine, however, strength of alpha oscillations was significantly reduced. For the Flanker task, in the Muse data, the stimulus-locked ERP components were less visible as compared to standard EEG, still the N200 was clearly expressed for the correct trials. Interestingly, in the incorrect trials, time-locked to the response there was the same negative Ne component visible as for the standard experiment. Our results reveal that the Muse device is suitable to obtain event-related potentials – even from interpolated electrode channels. Advanced preprocessing and artifact removal algorithms specifically targeting such devices with only a few and peripheral channels might help to better isolate ERP components of interest. It remains the challenge to develop devices and procedures for online tactile testing.

item.title: The Impact of Attention on Speech Entrainment in Clinical High-Risk for Psychosis Individuals
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Language comprehension is disrupted in schizophrenia and early-stage psychosis, but the contributions of bottom-up and top-down processing remain unclear. In the current electroencephalography (EEG) study, we investigated speech entrainment in a sample of n=21 individuals at clinical high-risk for psychosis (CHR-P) and n=25 healthy controls (HCs). Continuous speech was presented through an audiobook in three listening conditions: (1) “Active”, in which participants attended to speech; (2) “Passive”, in which participants passively listened to the audiobook while performing a concurrent visual Flanker task; and (3) “Passive-reversed”, in which participants listened to an unintelligible time-reversed and noise-vocoded version of the audiobook while performing the Flanker task. Mutual Information (MI) analyses were used to assess shared information between the speech amplitude envelope and neural oscillations in the delta (0.25-3 Hz), theta (4.5-6.5 Hz), and alpha (7-10 Hz) frequency ranges. Sensor-level and source-level results indicate stronger delta entrainment in the Active vs. Passive conditions across groups. However, compared to controls, CHR-Ps showed reduced theta entrainment in auditory cortices, independent of condition, and decreased alpha entrainment in the Passive vs. Active condition. The findings point to theta entrainment deficits in CHR-Ps during continuous speech processing, indexing a bottom-up impairment. In contrast, delta and alpha entrainment in CHR-Ps were modulated by attention. Together, these findings highlight that both bottom-up and top-down impairments contribute to speech entrainment deficits in CHR-Ps.

item.title: Neuroimaging Correlates of Adolescent Substance Use: A Systematic Review of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background: Neuroimaging may help characterize brain and contextual factors associated with substance use during development. The ABCD study supports investigation of developmental pathways relevant to substance use [1]. Objective: To synthesize original ABCD publications examining MRI measures in relation to substance use and substance-related exposures. Methods: The authors screened all 2,700 publications in the ABCD corpus. Original empirical articles reporting an MRI measure of any modality and a substance use variable were eligible; methodological, conceptual, review, and commentary articles were excluded. Imaging modality, brain measures, substances, design, and association direction were extracted for descriptive synthesis. Results: The evidence considered spans morphology, white matter microstructure, resting-state connectivity, and task activation. Findings concerning youth initiation, prenatal exposure, and familial liability address distinct developmental questions. Family history and stressful life events feature in the white matter literature [2]. Findings vary by modality, exposure definition, and temporal direction, and include null associations. Conclusions: The literature suggests distributed and context-dependent neuroimaging associations. Observational designs, overlapping participants, confounding, and analytic heterogeneity limit causal interpretation and assessment of independent replication. The findings support further longitudinal investigation but do not establish a validated MRI screening tool.

item.title: Investigating the Association of Physical Activity and Muscular Fitness with Structural Brain Changes and Cognitive Performance
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background Physical activity (PA) is a modifiable factor linked to cognitive decline, but its relationship with structural brain changes remains inconsistent. We studied associations of self-reported PA and handgrip strength with brain structure and cognition. Methods We examined middle-aged to elderly participants from the population-based Hamburg City Health Study, who underwent brain MRI and cognitive testing. PA was assessed via questionnaires (overall PA, sport participation, strength training frequency), and handgrip strength indexed muscular fitness. MRI markers included among others peak width of skeletonized mean diffusivity (PSMD), cortical thickness, and structural connectivity metrics. Cognition was assessed with CERAD-Plus subtests. Associations were examined using multivariable linear regression and mediation analysis. Results Among 2,618 participants (mean age 64 ± 8.3 years; 44% female), higher handgrip strength was associated with lower PSMD (β=-0.117, 95% CI [-0.194, -0.041]), greater cortical thickness (β = 0.100, 95% CI [0.019, 0.181]), and faster processing speed (β=-0.155, 95% CI [-0.234, -0.076]). Self-reported PA showed no associations with brain structure. Sport participation was associated with faster processing speed (β=-0.059, 95% CI [-0.105, -0.014]), better executive function (β=-0.045, 95% CI [-0.088, -0.002]), and better verbal memory (β = 0.052, 95% CI [0.007, 0.097]). PSMD partially mediated the association between handgrip strength and processing speed (ab=-0.008, 95% CI [-0.019, -0.001]). Conclusions Handgrip strength, unlike self-reported PA, was associated with brain structure and cognitive performance, highlighting the importance of PA assessment modality in brain health research. Mediation of associations between handgrip strength and cognition by PSMD suggest white matter microstructural injury as one pathway linking neuromuscular and cognitive function. Clinical Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT03934957.

item.title: Impairment of mental time travel in patients with depressive disorders: Neural mechanisms and individual-level identification based on default mode network connectivity
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background Mental time travel (MTT) enables re-experiencing past and pre-experiencing future events. Impairment in MTT is a core cognitive feature of major depressive disorder (MDD), but its neural mechanisms involving default mode network (DMN) functional connectivity remain unclear. Methods Thirty-six MDD patients and 36 healthy controls (HC) completed an adapted Autobiographical Memory Test to assess MTT. Resting-state fMRI examined DMN functional connectivity. Brain–behavior correlations used Spearman rank with Holm–Bonferroni correction. A support vector machine (SVM) classifier and support vector regression (SVR) evaluated individual discriminative and predictive values of identified connectivity features. Results Patients showed significantly reduced specificity in past recall and future imagination, with lower emotional valence, field perspective, and intensity. Resting-state connectivity revealed dissociated DMN patterns: weakened right anterior supramarginal gyrus–frontal pole, left frontal pole–posterior parietal, and hippocampus–lingual/cerebellar connections; enhanced left medial prefrontal–occipital and dorsal medial prefrontal–frontal pole connections. In HC, frontoparietal connectivity correlated with visual perspective; in patients, enhanced prefrontal connectivity negatively correlated with negative valence. Machine learning achieved 94.4% accuracy (AUC = 0.971) in classifying MDD vs HC, with frontal pole connections most discriminative. DMN connectivity significantly predicted individual specificity and neutral valence. Conclusions MTT impairment in MDD reflects system-level DMN imbalance and functional reorganization, providing neural targets for interventions. High individual classification accuracy supports DMN connectivity as a potential biomarker.

item.title: Metformin Preserves Regional Brain Glucose Uptake, Structure, and Functional Connectivity in Adults with Insulin Resistance.
item.description:
The Journal of clinical investigation
Background Dementia is a rapidly expanding public health problem with major socio-economic burden. Insulin resistance (IR) is a prevalent but modifiable risk factor for dementia, yet its effects on brain structure, functional connectivity, and metabolism remain incompletely understood. Methods Regional brain glucose uptake (PET), volumes (MRI), functional connectivity (fMRI), and cognition (NIH Toolbox) was measured in 72 adults with or without markers of IR. To evaluate reversibility of IR-associated brain deficits, forty older adults with IR were randomized to forty weeks of metformin or placebo, and brain measures were repeated. As a proof-of-concept experiment, we developed a conditional brain-specific insulin receptor knockout mouse and assessed brain mitochondrial function and cognition. Results In older adults with markers of IR is associated with diminished total and regional brain volumes in areas critical for neuronal connectivity, memory, and learning, including cerebral white matter and the hippocampus. Reduced functional connectivity between brain regions detrimental for cognition was also noted. Further, we demonstrated that ATP production, essential for neuronal connectivity, was diminished in neuron-specific insulin receptor knockout mice accompanied by deficits in hippocampal- and prefrontal-dependent tasks. Forty weeks of metformin improved systemic insulin sensitivity concurrent to preserved brain glucose uptake, volume, and functional connectivity within specific regions central to decision-making and learning. Metformin was also associated with an improved composite measure of processing speed and working memory. Conclusion These findings highlight IR as a key regulator of brain metabolism and support the concept that insulin sensitization can prevent neurobiological deficits in older people with IR.

item.title: Annual Research Review: A probe into sensitive periods - how the developmental timing of adverse childhood experiences influences brain structure and function - a systematic review.
item.description:
Journal of child psychology and psychiatry, and allied disciplines
It is proposed that adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) - potent predictors of mental illness - exert time-dependent effects on neurodevelopment, reflecting periods of heightened neuroplasticity and developmental sensitivity. We systematically reviewed neuroimaging studies examining the role of timing in the association of ACE exposure with brain structure and function across the lifespan. Across 43 studies spanning childhood to adulthood, findings most consistently implicate earlier onset and longer duration of adversity in alterations to limbic and paralimbic regions, including the hippocampus, amygdala, cerebellum and global brain measures. However, evidence for discrete sensitive periods is mixed and varies by brain system, outcome and analytic approach, with no consistent pattern of sensitive periods emerging across adversity types and functional neuroimaging studies remaining comparatively limited. Progress in the field is further constrained by substantial conceptual and methodological heterogeneity, including inconsistent operationalisation of sensitive periods, reliance on retrospective ACE measures and predominantly cross-sectional designs. Moving forward, we argue that advancing the field will require reconceptualising sensitive periods as probabilistic, system-specific and shaped by the nature, timing and chronicity of adversity, rather than as fixed developmental windows. Integrating longitudinal assessment of adversity and neurodevelopment with measures of the neurobiological processes underlying plasticity may help determine whether sensitive periods are better characterised by underlying neuroplasticity than chronological age alone. Improved understanding of these developmental processes may ultimately help inform the timing and targeting of preventive and therapeutic interventions for young people exposed to adversity.

item.title: Stimulus-specific recruitment of human amygdala neurons predicts episodic memory encoding success.
item.description:
Nature neuroscience
Controlling whether an experience is encoded into long-term memory and thus later remembered is a crucial aspect of memory. Here we examined single-neuron activity in the human brain while participants formed memories for novel visual stimuli and later retrieved them with confidence ratings. Category-selective amygdala neurons exhibited elevated firing during encoding of later remembered items relative to later forgotten items. This effect was predictive of the episodic aspect of the memory, was restricted to the preferred category of each cell, emerged earlier and was stronger in the amygdala compared to the hippocampus, and did not depend on stimulus valence and arousal. Successful memory formation was accompanied by enhanced spike-field coherence between the activity of amygdala category cells and hippocampal field potentials. These findings demonstrate that stimulus-specific recruitment of the amygdala predicts memory formation and suggest category cells in the right amygdala as a target for interventions to treat disorders affecting episodic memory in humans.

item.title: Visuospatial attention modulates audiovisual temporal perception: Context-dependent associations between prestimulus alpha lateralization and perceptual reports.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Audiovisual temporal perception depends on the timing of sensory events and on preparatory attention. We examined how visuospatial cueing affects explicit synchrony judgments and sound-induced flash illusions, and how prestimulus EEG relates to these perceptual reports. In Experiment 1 (N = 39), participants judged beep-flash synchrony across auditory- and visual-leading stimulus onset asynchronies (SOAs). In Experiment 2 (N = 36), they reported flashes in fusion and fission conditions across SOAs and corresponding references. Experiment 1 showed a Cue validity × SOA interaction, with more synchrony reports on valid trials at -100 and +50 ms. Cueing shifted the point of subjective simultaneity among 21 participants with reliable fits. Trial-level posterior alpha lateralization was associated with synchrony reports as a function of Cue validity. In Experiment 2, valid cues reduced raw fusion reports at -100, -50, and +100 ms. A Cue validity × SOA interaction persisted for reference-adjusted fusion scores, whereas neither raw nor adjusted fission showed a corresponding interaction. The association between reference-adjusted alpha lateralization and fusion reports varied with Cue validity and SOA, although a direct comparison with the visual reference did not establish an illusion-specific association. These EEG-behavior associations were stable after accounting for temporal progression, preceding trials, cue side, and an ocular-sensitive EEG proxy. Together, the findings indicate timing- and context-dependent effects of visuospatial attention on audiovisual temporal perception and identify preparatory posterior alpha lateralization as a correlate of subsequent reports.

item.title: Distinct neural patterns of valence and arousal in the developing brain: A representational similarity analysis of MEG.
item.description:
NeuroImage
How children and adolescents encode the affective meaning of visual stimuli remains poorly understood. A key reason is that valence and arousal are inherently correlated across affective stimuli and thus confounded in the categorical contrasts mostly used in emotion research. Here, in a secondary analysis of a previously collected MEG dataset, we dissociate the contributions of valence and arousal in emotional processing by applying partial representational similarity analysis (RSA) to magnetoencephalography (MEG) data from 57 typically developing children and adolescents (5 - 18 years old) viewing pictures from the Nencki Affective Picture System. Source-localized responses were first estimated on a volumetric grid, after which we tested, across regions and time windows, whether similarity in neural activity patterns tracked similarity in valence or arousal ratings while controlling for their shared variance. Valence emerged as the primary organizing dimension of neural representations in this sample, with effects detectable in frontotemporal and salience regions within the first 100 ms and sustained over time in the lateral prefrontal cortex. These responses formed a distributed representational network that progressively engaged higher-order evaluative regions. In contrast, arousal contributed transiently through a distinct network that only intermittently overlapped with valence-related activity. Together, these findings indicate that valence predominantly structures affective representations in this pediatric sample, whereas arousal exerts a weaker and more limited influence. This work provides an initial characterization of affective representational structure in this sample of children and adolescents, that if replicated, may inform future reference framework for identifying deviations associated with conditions such as autism spectrum disorder.

item.title: Spectral-spatial Modeling of Neural Couplings in Functional Connectivity of Motor Networks.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Background Functional neural connectivity reflects coordinated interactions within brain networks in both health and disease. Phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) is widely used for this purpose, but its pairwise formulations overlook spatially distributed, spectrally correlated structures in neural activity that arises from complex brain circuits. New method We developed a spectral-spatial generalized linear model (SS-GLM) to characterize the high-frequency response as the integrated outcome of multiple low-frequency phase sources across channels and frequencies. Our method also utilizes a regularization strategy to mitigate predictor collinearity and spurious effects for stable attribution of network-level coupling estimates. Results Validation was performed using both synthetic data and human motor network recordings from 25 patients with Parkinson's disease undergoing deep brain stimulation (DBS) surgery. In synthetic analyses, SS-GLM accurately recovered ground-truth coupling configurations under multiple plausible scenarios. In real data, the framework revealed coherent cortico-subthalamic coupling patterns across distinct motor tasks that aligned with clinically effective DBS contacts and their anatomical organization. Comparison with existing methods Conventional pairwise PAC metrics, such as the modulation index and GLM assess interactions in isolation. In contrast, SS-GLM jointly models distributed predictors and yields spatially localized, spectrally specific coupling estimates that also achieve stronger correspondence with clinical stimulation outcomes. Conclusions This work offers a principled and extensible framework for advancing functional connectivity analyses, with improved interpretability of network-level interactions, enhanced robustness to confounds, and broad potential for future applications in systems neuroscience and neuro-engineering research.

item.title: The Entangled Loop: Emotion, interference and hierarchy in the architecture of consciousness.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Why does consciousness feel like something, and why is experience unified rather than fragmented? We propose that these properties arise from an entangled trefoil of emotion, interference-based inference and hierarchical orchestration, shaped by the thermodynamic constraint that living systems must remain far from equilibrium using limited energy. Emotion compresses actions into valenced signals of what matters, while a pleasure cycle schedules competing biological needs through predictive wanting and satiety organised around the true hedonic outcome of liking. Hierarchical orchestrating regions integrate and broadcast information through interference between classical coupled oscillators, shaped by the spectral gaps of the connectome driven by long-range exceptions to local cortical wiring. The architecture of the Entangled Loop consists of three inseparable strands, each continually constraining the other two, with the one operator linking computational possibilities to the arrow of time and energetic cost of running them. Evidence suggests that the same three signatures emerge independently in large language models trained on human language, but as shadows of the generating architecture rather than evidence of consciousness. The trefoil predicts a distinctive human vulnerability because our abundance of rare long-range connections promotes more computation for less energy while making the architecture more fragile. Neuropsychiatric disorders could therefore arise from perturbations entering through any strand and propagating through the others, while the more robust architecture of other species may help explain why animal models reproduce human psychiatric disorders poorly. Sustaining and restoring flexible entanglement in the Entangled Loop may provide mechanistic routes towards flourishing.

item.title: Altered developmental trajectories in neurodevelopmental disorders: mechanisms, human models and translational perspectives.
item.description:
Journal of neural transmission (Vienna, Austria : 1996)
Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) are clinically and genetically heterogeneous conditions often studied through diagnostic categories, causal genes, synaptic dysfunction or end-stage phenotypes. Although these approaches remain essential, they do not fully capture the developmental nature of NDD pathophysiology. This review proposes a trajectory-first framework in which NDDs are interpreted as disorders of altered developmental progression. From this perspective, the key question is not only which gene, pathway, cell type, or synapse is affected, but when, where and how neurodevelopment begins to diverge. We discuss mechanisms of trajectory divergence, including altered developmental timing, cell-state and lineage disruption, selective cellular vulnerability, epigenetic and signaling dysregulation, cytoskeletal and morphogenetic abnormalities, synaptic maturation defects, excitability changes and network-level alterations. We then examine how human systems, including fetal and post-mortem atlases, iPSC-derived models, cortical organoids, assembloids, functional readouts and patient-level phenotypes, can be integrated to reconstruct developmental trajectories across biological scales. Representative NDD genes and syndromes illustrate that distinct divergence points may later converge on shared functional or clinical outcomes, including altered excitation/inhibition balance, abnormal network activity, epilepsy, language delay, intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder features or motor dysfunction. Finally, we discuss limitations and perspectives for trajectory-based stratification and biomarker discovery. Rather than acting as static diagnostic readouts, future biomarkers should aim to capture developmental state, timing, divergence, convergence, compensation and response to intervention.
